Content:
We can multiply matrices by numbers. This type of multiplication is known as scalar multiplication. Here, a scalar is just a number.

Content:
For example, consider the matrix
[MATH: [1|3; 2|4]]

Content:
To multiply [MATH: {A}] by the scalar [MATH: 2,] we just multiply each entry of [MATH: {A}] by [MATH: 2\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: 2A|= 2[1|3; 2|4]; = [2 ⋅ 1|2 ⋅ 3; 2 ⋅ 2|2 ⋅ 4]; = [2|6; 4|8]]

Content:
In general, to multiply a [MATH: m \times n] matrix [MATH: A] by a scalar [MATH: c,] we multiply each entry of [MATH: A] by [MATH: c] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: [a_{11}|a_{12}|…|a_{1n}; a_{21}|a_{22}|…|a_{2n}; ⋮|⋮|⋱|⋮; a_{m1}|a_{m2}|…|a_{mn}]]

Since scalar multiplication is done entry-wise, it obeys the same kind of rules as multiplication of real numbers.

[MATH: c (A \pm B) = c A \pm c B]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We can multiply matrices by numbers. This type of multiplication is known as scalar multiplication. Here, a scalar is just a number.

Content:
For example, consider the matrix
[MATH: [1|3; 2|4]]

Content:
To multiply [MATH: {A}] by the scalar [MATH: 2,] we just multiply each entry of [MATH: {A}] by [MATH: 2\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: 2A|= 2[1|3; 2|4]; = [2 ⋅ 1|2 ⋅ 3; 2 ⋅ 2|2 ⋅ 4]; = [2|6; 4|8]]

Content:
In general, to multiply a [MATH: m \times n] matrix [MATH: A] by a scalar [MATH: c,] we multiply each entry of [MATH: A] by [MATH: c] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: [a_{11}|a_{12}|…|a_{1n}; a_{21}|a_{22}|…|a_{2n}; ⋮|⋮|⋱|⋮; a_{m1}|a_{m2}|…|a_{mn}]]

---

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We multiply each entry of [MATH: A] by [MATH: -2,] as follows:

[MATH: − 2A|= − 2[2|− 1; 4|7]; = [− 2 ⋅ 2|− 2 ⋅ (− 1); − 2 ⋅ 4|− 2 ⋅ 7]; = [− 4|2; − 8|− 14]]

\right\rbrack,]
where [MATH: {A} =
\left\lbrack

2 & 6 & 8 \
12 & 0 & -4
}
\right\rbrack]
and [MATH: k] is a scalar, calculate the value of [MATH: k.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To express [MATH: kA,] we multiply each entry of [MATH: A] by [MATH: k,] as follows:

[MATH: kA|= k ⋅ [2|6|8; 12|0|− 4]; = [2k|6k|8k; 12k|0|− 4k]]

Now, we set the above result equal to the matrix given for [MATH: kA] in the problem statement:

[MATH: \left\lbrack
\matrix {
2k & 6k & 8k \
12k & 0 & -4k
}
\right\rbrack
=
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
1 & 3 & 4 \
6 & 0 & -2
}
\right\rbrack]

We can solve for [MATH: k] by equating any two corresponding (nonzero) elements. Let's choose the top-left elements, [MATH: 2k] and [MATH: 1.] Equating these elements, we get

[MATH: 2k|= 1; k|= (1)/(2).]

Note: We would still get the same result if we chose any other two corresponding (nonzero) elements.

Item 8 — Tutorial: Properties of Scalar Multiplication of Matrices

Content:
Since scalar multiplication is done entry-wise, it obeys the same kind of rules as multiplication of real numbers.

Content:
For example, for any numbers [MATH: c_1, c_2] and any matrix [MATH: A,] we can perform scalar multiplication in any order:

Content:
[MATH: c_1 (c_2 A) = (c_1 c_2) A = c_2 (c_1 A)]

Content:
Moreover, we can distribute a matrix over the sum or difference of scalars:
[MATH: (c_1 \pm c_2)A = c_1A \pm c_2A]

Content:
We can also distribute scalar multiplication over the sum or difference of two matrices:
[MATH: c (A \pm B) = c A \pm c B]

Item 9 — Example: Calculating a Linear Combination of Two Matrices

Example Prompt:
Calculate [MATH: 2 {A} + \dfrac{1}{2} {B}], where
[MATH: [1|5; 1|2]] and [MATH: {B}=
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
0 & 2 \
4 & 2
}
\right\rbrack
.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We multiply each entry of [MATH: A] by [MATH: 2] and each entry of [MATH: B] by [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2},] and then add the resulting matrices, as follows:

[MATH: 2A + (1)/(2)B|= 2[1|5; 1|2] + (1)/(2)[0|2; 4|2]; = [2 ⋅ 1|2 ⋅ 5; 2 ⋅ 1|2 ⋅ 2] + [(1)/(2) ⋅ 0|(1)/(2) ⋅ 2; (1)/(2) ⋅ 4|(1)/(2) ⋅ 2]; = [2|10; 2|4] + [0|1; 2|1]; = [2 + 0|10 + 1; 2 + 2|4 + 1]; = [2|11; 4|5]]

---
